summary: Defines an extensible format and MIME type for mail operators to report feedback about received email, as a machine-readable replacement for existing report formats. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A form for saying 'this mail was spam' that computers understand.

questions: what is the abuse reporting format
how do email spam reports work
subtitle: A standard, machine-readable email format for telling another mail operator about spam, fraud, viruses and similar problems.

tldr.problem: Mail operators were exchanging abuse reports in many different home-made formats, so every receiver had to write custom software to read each one.
tldr.mechanism: A report is a three-part MIME multipart/report message: human-readable text, a machine-readable message/feedback-report part of header-style fields, and the original message or its headers.
tldr.outcome: It gives operators one extensible format with IANA registries for new fields and feedback types. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 6650.

today: RFC 5965 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 6650, so check that RFC alongside this one. The format is defined here together with its IANA registries for feedback types and report header fields.

sections.title: Why a Standard Report Format
sections.content:
As spam grew, mail operators began swapping abuse reports with each other. The problem was that each operator defined its own format, so receivers had to write custom software to interpret each one. Other operators used further formats to give non-abuse feedback about processed email.

RFC 5965 defines a standard, extensible format by creating the message/feedback-report MIME type, used inside the multipart/report type from RFC 3462. It is primarily an Abuse Reporting Format (ARF), but it also covers direct feedback from end-user mail clients and reports of some types of virus activity. The RFC notes that earlier attempts in this area had not been successful and hopes this one will fare better.

Where reports are sent, how their contents are validated and how trust is established are outside its scope. The format SHOULD NOT be used for other kinds of reports.
sections.plainLanguage: Before this, every mailroom wrote complaints in its own style. This RFC gives everyone one shared form so a complaint can be understood by anybody.

sections.title: What a Report Must Do
sections.content:
The RFC lists four requirements. A report must be both human and machine readable. It must enclose a copy of the original message (header and body) or at least the message header, so the receiver can handle it properly. The machine-readable section must let the generator share meta-data with the receiver. And the format must be extensible.

The stated purpose is to inform mail operators about email abuse originating from their networks and about potential problems with the perceived quality of their outbound mail, such as a service provider sending mail that attracts automated abuse detection.
sections.plainLanguage: A good complaint has a note a person can read, a form a computer can read, and a copy of the problem letter attached.

sections.title: The Three-Part Report Message
sections.content:
A feedback report is a MIME message whose top-level type is multipart/report, with the report-type parameter set to feedback-report. It has three parts, and all three MUST be included.

  • Part 1 is a human-readable description of the report.
  • Part 2 is the machine-readable message/feedback-report section, carrying meta-data that may not be obvious from the original message.
  • Part 3 is either the whole original message (message/rfc822) or its entire header block (text/rfc822-headers). Redaction is allowed for privacy or legal reasons, but the RFC RECOMMENDS including the whole message unmodified, because changes can impede forensic work.

Each report MUST relate to a single email message; summary and aggregate formats are out of scope. The Subject SHOULD match the reported message, differing at most by a forwarding prefix such as FW:. When acting on a report, recipients SHOULD use part 3 first, then part 2, and SHOULD NOT use part 1 if it conflicts with the others.
sections.plainLanguage: The report is a package with three things inside: a friendly note, a form for computers, and the junk letter itself as proof.

sections.title: The Fields in the Machine-Readable Part
sections.content:
Part 2 is a list of fields written like mail header fields. They are semantically different from real headers, so they SHOULD NOT be repeated as header fields of the report message. Receivers MUST NOT assume the assertions are accurate, because they are not necessarily verifiable.

Required, exactly once: Feedback-Type (the type of report), User-Agent (name and version of the generating software, documentation only) and Version (set to 1 in this specification).

Optional, at most once: Original-Envelope-Id, Original-Mail-From, Arrival-Date, Reporting-MTA, Source-IP and Incidents (an unsigned 32-bit integer; if absent, the report covers a single incident). The historic Received-Date SHOULD be accepted as Arrival-Date, but if both are present the report is malformed.

Optional, repeatable: Authentication-Results, Original-Rcpt-To (SHOULD be repeated for every SMTP recipient), Reported-Domain and Reported-URI. The RFC adds that the generator's choice of reported domain or URI is unspecified, so the receiver cannot be sure how it was chosen.
sections.plainLanguage: The computer form has boxes like 'what kind of problem', 'which program wrote this', and 'where did the letter come from'. Some boxes must be filled in and some are optional.

sections.title: Extending the Format
sections.content:
Extensibility comes from two IANA registries: one for feedback types, used with the Feedback-Type field, and one for report header fields. New registrations follow the Specification Required policy, are optional by default, and must be published in an open specification such as an RFC. New required fields would need a new version of the specification. Version numbers do not change when fields are registered.

To keep things interoperable, implementers MUST ignore any fields or report types they do not support. Experimental types and fields MUST only be used between administrative domains that have agreed to use them.

The initial feedback types are abuse, fraud, virus and other. The registered media type has no parameters, and its encoding notes say 7bit encoding is sufficient and MUST be used. If a message claims to be an ARF report but violates the syntax, the agent SHOULD ignore or reject it, and any rejection notice SHOULD identify the specific cause.
sections.plainLanguage: The form can grow new boxes later, but only through an official list. If your computer does not know a box, it just skips it.

sections.title: Trust, Privacy and Abuse of Reports
sections.content:
The format says nothing about whether a report is true. An unvetted report could be wrong, incomplete or deliberately false in any of its three parts, so the RFC suggests vetting the origin, for example with S/MIME, DKIM, SPF or Sender ID, before any automated action. S/MIME is called the strongest, but it can interfere with code written specifically for multipart/report parsing.

Other concerns the RFC lists:

  • Attackers may send very large or malformed reports to exploit parsers, so implementations SHOULD be robust.
  • Reports can reveal private information, such as a valid address on a mailing list, so generators may redact, at the price of a less useful report.
  • Automatic generation, for example from a honeypot address, can be exploited to flood a recipient with reports.
  • Attachments SHOULD be handled as unverified, potentially hostile data.
  • The User-Agent field is trivially forged and SHOULD NOT be interpreted by recipients.
  • Being liberal about related fields such as Received-Date and Arrival-Date lets an attacker craft confusing reports.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can send a complaint form, even a fake one. So before you act on it, check that it really came from who it says, and treat anything attached with care.
